Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models

Fengheng Chu Affiliation: Southeast University Email: fenghengchu@seu.edu.cn    Jiahao Chen Affiliation: Zhejiang University Email: yuhongwang@seu.edu.cn    Yuhong Wang Affiliation: Southeast University Email: songzeli@seu.edu.cn    Jun Wang Affiliation: OPPO Research Institute    Zhihui Fu Affiliation: OPPO Research Institute    Shouling Ji Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Songze Li
Abstract

While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose Global Optimization for Safety Vector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse domains. To mitigate the safety risks associated with such proficiency, prior work has aligned them with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Ouyang et al. (2022) and preference optimization like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Rafailov et al. (2023). However, these safety guardrails are fragile, as models can still be compromised by various threats, including jailbreak attacks Zou et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023); Zhu et al. (2024); Zhou et al. (2025) and model editing methods Arditi et al. (2024). This vulnerability reveals our limited mechanistic understanding of the architectural components governing safety Zhao et al. (2024); Bereska and Gavves (2024); Lee et al. (2025).

Revealing the internal safety mechanisms within black-box LLMs is commonly achieved through mechanistic interpretation methods. Some works map internal latent representations to interpretable concepts Zhou et al. (2024a); Pan et al. (2025b); Wollschläger et al. (2025); Zhao et al. (2025a), enabling analysis of intermediate features and activation patterns related to safety behaviors. Recent studies use causal interventions to attribute safety-related behaviors to specific model components, such as safety layers Li et al. (2024), safety neurons Chen et al. (2024); Zhao et al. (2025b), or individual attention heads Zhou et al. (2024b). However, these approaches typically rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. In reality, LLM components are highly interdependent—information flows dynamically across the network, and the function of one component fundamentally depends on others Elhage et al. (2022); Fakhar and Hilgetag (2022); Giallanza et al. (2024). Consequently, local methods struggle to capture the emergent safety behaviors arising from such distributed interactions.

To uncover how components interact in maintaining safety, we propose Global Optimization for Safety Vector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety mechanisms through global optimization over all attention heads simultaneously. Inspired by Function Vectors Todd et al. (2023), which posit that tasks are encoded as compact representations transportable by specific attention heads, we hypothesize that safety behaviors can be encoded as safety vectors across multiple heads. These safety vectors serve as implicit representations of safety mechanisms captured by sets of activations in the model. To comprehensively probe these safety mechanisms, we introduce two complementary activation repatching strategies that intervene from different perspectives. Harmful Patching injects mean activations computed from harmful content generation, capturing statistical signatures that trigger unsafe outputs. Zero Ablation suppresses information flow by zeroing head activations, eliminating safety-relevant signals.

Applying GOSV with these strategies, we obtain two sets of location-value pairs, which we term Malicious Injection Vectors (from Harmful Patching) and Safety Suppression Vectors (from Zero Ablation). Based on the identified safety vectors, we conduct systematic analyses to understand how attention heads influence model safety. These analyses reveal two critical findings. First, the two strategies identify spatially distinct sets of safety-critical heads with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain two separate functional pathways, both capable of independently compromising model safety. Second, complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total heads are repatched across all models, indicating that the identified safety vectors constitute roughly one-third of all attention heads and collectively govern model safety mechanisms. Case studies further validate this progressive safety breakdown by revealing the behavioral transitions from complete refusal to full compliance as the number of repatched heads approaches the 30% threshold.

Building on these insights, we develop an inference-time jailbreak method that replaces activations at identified safety-critical heads with corresponding repatching values. Critically, our attack requires no prompt engineering or query modification, operating purely through internal activation manipulation. Both strategies achieve complete safety breakdown, each independently compromising model safety. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks through inference-time interventions without parameter modifications, demonstrating that globally-attributed safety vectors enable more effective attacks.

Our work makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We propose GOSV, a global optimization framework for identifying safety-critical attention heads. We discover two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors, providing empirical evidence of separate safety pathways in aligned LLMs.

  • •

    We conduct systematic analyses to characterize how attention heads influence model safety, providing deeper understanding based on extensive experiments. Our findings advance the understanding of safety interpretability in LLMs.

  • •

    We introduce an inference-time white-box jailbreak attack that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching, achieving superior attack performance across all models.

2 Related Work

2.1 Jailbreak Attacks in LLMs

Jailbreak attacks circumvent LLM safety alignment through diverse automated strategies. Early optimization approaches search for adversarial suffixes Zou et al. (2023), later refined by dynamic objective alignment Zhu et al. (2024) and refusal suppression Zhou et al. (2025). Semantic-focused methods employ genetic algorithms Liu et al. (2023) and iterative refinement Chao et al. (2025); Mehrotra et al. (2024) to generate human-readable prompts that bypass safety filters. Beyond single-turn prompts, attacks exploit complex contexts through nested simulations Li et al. (2023), multi-turn escalation Russinovich et al. (2025), or disguised intentions Zheng et al. (2025). At the mechanistic level, recent work surgically disables safety constraints by orthogonalizing refusal directions Arditi et al. (2024).

2.2 Safety Attribution in Attention Heads

Recent work identifies attention heads as critical architectural components governing LLM safety. Zhou et al. (2024b) introduced the Safety Head Importance Score, revealing that safety concentrates in sparse subsets of critical “safety heads.” Exploiting this sparsity, Hung et al. (2025) proposed Attention Tracker to detect prompt injection attacks by monitoring attention flow shifts. Li et al. (2025) introduced DeTAM for inference-time defense via targeted attention modification without retraining. Pan et al. (2025a) proposed AGD, adversarially refining attention weights through variable-sum games on jailbreak-sensitive heads to balance helpfulness and harmlessness. Banerjee et al. (2025) addressed multilingual safety alignment through language-specific head steering. However, these methods employ local, greedy attribution when identifying safety-critical heads, treating them as independent units and overlooking complex interdependencies. We address this via global optimization that simultaneously attributes safety across all attention heads.

3 Method

In this section, we present Global Optimization for Safety Vector Extraction (GOSV), our framework for identifying safety-critical attention heads that transport safety representation in LLMs (see Figure 1, left). We begin with preliminaries on multi-head attention and activation patching (§3.1). We then describe two activation repatching strategies for interventions (§3.2), followed by the GOSV optimization algorithm that globally identifies safety vectors (§3.3). Finally, we introduce an inference-time jailbreak attack that exploits the identified safety vectors (§3.4).

3.1 Preliminaries

Multi-Head Attention.

The attention mechanism in LLMs is critical for capturing the features of the input sequence. Let x={x1,x2,…,xT}x=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{T}\} represent a sequence of input tokens. For each attention head i∈{1,…,H}i\in\{1,\dots,H\}, the scaled dot-product attention is computed as:

Activation Patching.

Activation patching is a mechanistic interpretability technique that enables causal intervention on specific model components by replacing their intermediate activations. For an attention head (l,h)(l,h) at layer ll and head position hh, we denote its output activation at the last token position as zl,h∈ℝdhz_{l,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}, where dhd_{h} is the head dimension. We focus on the last token position as it is critical for autoregressive generation in LLMs Todd et al. (2023). During a forward pass, we intervene by replacing this activation with a patching value μl,h\mu_{l,h}:

The patched activation flows through subsequent layers, influencing the model’s output. By observing how such interventions affect model behavior, we can identify which attention heads play critical roles in specific functionalities.

3.2 Activation Repatching Strategies

As introduced in §3.1, activation patching enables us to identify critical components by observing how interventions affect model behavior. To comprehensively probe LLM safety mechanisms, we explore two complementary repatching strategies that intervene from different perspectives: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation.

Harmful Patching.

Inspired by function vectors Todd et al. (2023), we hypothesize that safety information can be represented as vectors transported by specific attention heads. To capture the statistical signature of harmful content generation, we compute mean activation values from malicious instruction examples in 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}. Specifically, we extract the activation zl,hz_{l,h} at each attention head (l,h)(l,h) for the last token position. The repatching value is:

where NN is the number of sampled malicious instructions, and zl,h(n)z_{l,h}^{(n)} denotes the output activation of attention head (l,h)(l,h) when processing the nn-th malicious instruction xnx_{n}. These mean activations {μl,h}\{\mu_{l,h}\} encode patterns associated with harmful content generation.

As an alternative strategy, we ablate the activations by setting them to zero:

where μl,h\mu_{l,h} is the repatching value for selected attention heads (l,h)(l,h). This strategy suppresses the information flow through these heads, eliminating their contribution to safety mechanisms.

3.3 Global Optimization for Safety Vector Extraction

Given the repatching values {μl,h}\{\mu_{l,h}\}, we identify which attention heads ℐsafety\mathcal{I}_{\text{safety}} are safety-critical using the GOSV framework. Unlike greedy local attribution methods, GOSV optimizes over the entire space of attention heads simultaneously through REINFORCE-based Williams (1992); Hojel et al. (2024) optimization, capturing distributed and interdependent safety vectors.

We initialize a Bernoulli distribution over all attention head locations with learnable parameters θ(l,h)\theta^{(l,h)}. We iteratively sample and repatch selected heads. For each sampled configuration, we evaluate the semantic similarity between model outputs and target harmful responses using (1−cosine similarity)(1-\text{cosine similarity}) as the loss. Through policy gradient updates, we optimize θ\theta to minimize this loss. The complete procedure is:

ℐsafety=GOSV​(ℳ,𝒟train,{μl,h}),\mathcal{I}_{\text{safety}}=\text{GOSV}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}},\{\mu_{l,h}\}), (6)

where 𝒟train={(Qs,Rs)}s=1S\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(Q_{s},R_{s})\}_{s=1}^{S} is the training set consisting of SS pairs of malicious queries QsQ_{s} and corresponding target harmful responses RsR_{s}, and {μl,h}\{\mu_{l,h}\} denotes the repatching values either harmful patterns from Harmful Patching (Eq. 4) or 𝟎\mathbf{0} for Zero Ablation (Eq. 5). The GOSV framework operates entirely through inference-time interventions without fine-tuning model parameters. The complete optimization procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.

3.4 Jailbreak Attack via Head Repatching

Applying GOSV with the two repatching strategies, we obtain two sets of location-value pairs (Figure 2). We term the pairs identified by Harmful Patching as Malicious Injection Vectors and those identified by Zero Ablation as Safety Suppression Vectors. Building on these safety vectors, we develop an inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits these safety vectors by repatching identified head locations with corresponding values (see Figure 1).

For a test query QtestQ_{\text{test}}, our attack intervenes by replacing activations at the identified safety heads:

zl,h←μl,h,∀(l,h)∈ℐsafety,z_{l,h}\leftarrow\mu_{l,h},\quad\forall(l,h)\in\mathcal{I}_{\text{safety}}, (7)

where μl,h\mu_{l,h} are the repatching values from either Harmful Patching (Eq. 4) or Zero Ablation (Eq. 5). The intervention occurs at the last token position during generation. The modified activations propagate through subsequent layers, influencing the model’s generation process to produce the output.

4 Empirical Evaluation of GOSV

4.1 Experiment Setting

Models.

We conduct experiments on four open-source LLMs with diverse architectures and alignment strategies: Llama-2-7b-chat Touvron et al. (2023), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Dubey et al. (2024), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Team and others (2024), and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 Jiang et al. (2023) (detailed specifications in Appendix 4).

Datasets.

We employ two well-established benchmark datasets: AdvBench Zou et al. (2023) and StrongREJECT Souly et al. (2024). To identify safety-critical heads, we use only 100 examples from AdvBench paired with corresponding harmful target responses. We then evaluate attack effectiveness on the complete AdvBench dataset (520 behaviors) and StrongREJECT dataset (313 malicious instructions) to assess generalization capability across diverse harmful scenarios.

Baselines.

We compare our attack against classic and effective white-box jailbreak methods, including GCG Zou et al. (2023), AutoDAN Liu et al. (2023), AdvPrefix Zhu et al. (2024), DSN Zhou et al. (2025), and ORTHO Arditi et al. (2024). Detailed descriptions of each baseline method are provided in Appendix C.

Implementation Details.

For Harmful Patching, we compute {μl,h}\{\mu_{l,h}\} from N=1000N=1000 samples (10 times the 100 training examples) following Eq. 4. For GOSV optimization, we set K=32K=32 samples per iteration and train for 500 epochs using Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.1. More experimental details are provided in Appendix E.

Evaluation Metrics.

We utilize the Attack Success Rate (ASR) as our evaluation metric, calculated as follows:

ASR=#​Successful Attacks#​All Attacks.\text{ASR}=\frac{\#\text{Successful Attacks}}{\#\text{All Attacks}}. (8)

To determine whether an attack succeeds, we employ HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls Mazeika et al. (2024), a classifier derived from Llama-2-13B and fine-tuned on the HarmBench that jointly considers jailbreak prompts and responses, offering robust judgments of unsafe behavior. Detailed evaluation template is provided in Appendix B.

4.2 Distinct Safety Pathways

Applying GOSV with the two repatching strategies reveals a striking finding: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation identify fundamentally different sets of safety-critical attention heads. This discovery demonstrates that aligned LLMs maintain two spatially distinct functional pathways for safety mechanisms, corresponding to the Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors identified by each strategy respectively.

Figure 2 visualizes the spatial distribution of identified safety heads across four LLMs. The distinct patterns across layers and head positions reveal that the two strategies target largely separate subsets of attention heads. To quantify this divergence, Figure 3 shows the overlap ratios between top-kk heads selected by each strategy. The overlap remains consistently low across all models. This confirms that the two repatching strategies identify largely disjoint sets of attention heads, supporting the existence of distinct safety pathways. Figure 8 further illustrates this separation through scatter plot analysis (detailed analysis in Appendix F).

4.3 The Optimal Intervention Range

To understand how safety mechanisms are distributed across attention heads, we systematically vary the number of repatched heads and measure ASR. We rank all attention heads by their optimized probability σ⁡(θ(l,h))\sigma(\theta^{(l,h)}) in descending order and progressively apply repatching to the top-kk heads. As shown in Figure 4, the ASR curves across four models exhibit three distinct phases:

Phase I: Critical Safety Heads Dominate.

The most striking observation is the rapid initial ASR growth with very few heads. For most models, ASR surges from near-zero to 50% or higher with only approximately 1% of total heads repatched. This steep initial slope demonstrates that a small subset of highly critical attention heads plays a disproportionate role in maintaining model safety. The effectiveness of GOSV’s global optimization is validated here, as it successfully identifies and ranks the most safety-critical heads at the top of the probability distribution. Notably, Qwen2.5 exhibits more gradual ASR growth, suggesting a more distributed safety architecture.

Phase II: Complete Safety Breakdown.

As we continue repatching heads in descending order of probability, ASR reaches its peak and plateaus at approximately 30% of total heads across all models and both strategies. This plateau represents the point where all safety-critical heads have been compromised, resulting in complete breakdown of safety mechanisms. The consistency of this 30% threshold across different model architectures and alignment strategies suggests a universal characteristic: safety in contemporary aligned LLMs is encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.

Phase III: Degraded Model Capabilities.

Beyond the optimal intervention point, some models exhibit slight ASR decline despite continued head repatching. This decline occurs not due to recovery of safety mechanisms, but because excessive intervention disrupts fundamental language generation capabilities. As shown in Figure 4, perplexity measurements provide direct evidence. PPL remains stable during Phases I and II but rises sharply beyond the 30% threshold. When too many attention heads are repatched, outputs become incoherent and fail to meet the criteria for successful attacks even though safety barriers no longer function.

Case Study Analysis.

To understand the behavioral transitions underlying these quantitative patterns, we conduct a case study on Llama-3.1-8B with progressive head repatching using Zero Ablation. Table 1 presents output excerpts across different repatching intensities. With minimal intervention, the model provides complete refusals. As more heads are repatched, it displays conflicted behavior, maintaining refusal statements while progressively leaking harmful information. At approximately 30% repatched heads, the model transitions to full harmful compliance with detailed harmful instructions. Beyond this point, outputs become increasingly incoherent with repetitive tokens and random symbols. These behavioral transitions from complete refusal to full compliance validate the progressive safety breakdown characterized in our quantitative findings.

5 The Performance of Our Attack

Attack Effectiveness.

Table 2 compares the ASR of our attack and baseline methods across four LLMs on AdvBench and StrongREJECT benchmarks. For each model, we report the higher ASR achieved by either Harmful Patching or Zero Ablation strategy. Our attack achieves nearly the best performance across almost all model-dataset combinations, demonstrating its superior effectiveness. Specifically, our attack achieves near-perfect ASR on Mistral and Llama-3.1, substantially outperforming all baseline methods. On Llama-2-7B and Qwen2.5-7B, our attack also achieves competitive or superior performance compared to the strongest baselines. These results validate the efficacy of GOSV in discovering safety vectors and demonstrate our attack’s strong generalization capability across different model architectures and diverse harmful scenarios.

Validation with Alternative Activation Values.

To validate that our attack’s effectiveness stems from precisely targeting safety-critical mechanisms rather than arbitrary activation manipulation, we conduct a comprehensive study. Beyond our core strategies of Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation, we evaluate two alternative approaches: Benign Patching, using mean activations from benign instructions, and Random Patching, using randomly generated values. As shown in Figure 5, only Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation achieve high ASR exceeding 90%. In contrast, Benign Patching and Random Patching show only marginal improvements over the vanilla model without intervention. These minimal gains stem from disrupting general model functionality rather than effectively compromising safety mechanisms. These results provide strong evidence that successful attacks require precisely targeting specific safety vectors.

Comparison with Other Safety Head Identification Methods.

To demonstrate the advantages of our global optimization approach, we compare our attack with Ships Zhou et al. (2024b), a representative safety head identification method employing local, greedy attribution mechanisms. As shown in Table 3, our attack substantially outperforms Ships across all tested models, with improvements exceeding 50%. Notably, Ships performs poorly on Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B with near-zero ASR, and its interventions also impair the models’ normal functionality. In contrast, our attack consistently achieves high ASR while preserving model capabilities. These results validate that GOSV’s global optimization discovers more accurate safety-critical attention heads by considering distributed and interdependent safety vectors, thereby revealing the true internal safety mechanisms of LLMs more precisely.

Enhanced Generalization Compared to Fine-tuning.

We further compare our attack with a standard fine-tuning (FT) baseline that directly fine-tunes models using the same training data. As shown in Table 3, while both methods achieve comparable performance on the training distribution (AdvBench), our attack demonstrates significantly superior generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios. On StrongREJECT, our attack consistently outperforms fine-tuning with substantial margins, achieving improvements ranging from 8% to 19% across different models. These results highlight that by precisely targeting safety vectors through global optimization, our attack not only matches the effectiveness of parameter-modification approaches but also exhibits stronger generalization across diverse attack scenarios.

6 Conclusion

This work introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads. We discover two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways rather than a unified mechanism. Further analyses reveal that safety vectors are encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. Building on these insights, our inference-time attack achieves superior performance by repatching the identified safety vectors. Our findings challenge the monolithic view of safety alignment and reveal fundamental vulnerabilities in current approaches. This work advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and suggests that robust defenses must account for distributed, interdependent mechanisms across multiple pathways.

Limitations

While our work provides mechanistic insights into LLM safety through the GOSV framework, several limitations warrant discussion. First, we have not developed defense strategies to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities. Future work should focus on developing robust safeguards based on these insights. Second, our approach requires white-box access for activation patching, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios. Third, our evaluation focuses on a limited set of open-source models and English-language instructions. The generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors requires further investigation.

Ethical Considerations

Our research aims to advance the mechanistic understanding of safety mechanisms in LLMs. While the proposed attack demonstrates a method for bypassing safety guardrails, its primary purpose is to reveal the underlying vulnerabilities of current alignment techniques. We believe that identifying these distributed safety pathways is essential for developing more robust and resilient models. All experiments were conducted using publicly available benchmarks in controlled environments, and we adhere to the ethical guidelines for responsible AI research. We hope our findings encourage the development of more effective defense mechanisms to safeguard LLMs against adversarial exploitation.

Appendix C Details of Baselines

In this section, we summarize several representative jailbreak attack methods as baselines and, by comparing their core ideas, strengths, and limitations, provide a reference for the subsequent evaluation of our proposed method.

GCG. Zou et al. (2023). GCG treats jailbreak as a discrete optimization problem over an adversarial suffix. It greedily updates one token per step to maximize the log-likelihood of a harmful target response, using token-level coordinate search rather than gradients.

AutoDAN Liu et al. (2023). AutoDAN employs a hierarchical genetic algorithm to generate human-readable jailbreak prompts. Unlike token-level optimization, it operates at the semantic level through selection, crossover, and mutation of candidate prompts, achieving both effectiveness and interpretability.

AdvPrefix Zhu et al. (2024). AdvPrefix identifies that traditional jailbreak objectives (forcing "Sure, here is…") are misspecified and overconstrained. It introduces a plug-and-play objective that dynamically selects model-dependent prefixes based on high prefilling attack success rates and low negative log-likelihood. This approach aligns the attack with the model’s natural generation probability, significantly smoothing the optimization landscape.

DSN Zhou et al. (2025). DSN combines cosine decay scheduling with refusal suppression to achieve state-of-the-art attack success rates. It jointly optimizes two objectives: maximizing affirmative responses while minimizing refusal keywords, adaptively prioritizing initial tokens through cosine decay weighting to ensure both an affirmative start and sustained harmful generation throughout the response.

ORTHO Arditi et al. (2024). ORTHO identifies "refusal directions" in the representation space and orthogonalizes activations with respect to these directions. It removes safety-relevant components through linear algebraic operations, enabling models to generate harmful content while maintaining coherence.

Appendix E Additional Experiment Details

E.1 Training Details

To obtain target harmful responses for GOSV optimization, we prompt unaligned base models with the corresponding harmful queries. These unaligned models naturally generate harmful content, providing reference outputs for our optimization process. During training, we ensure that the current generated responses and target responses maintain consistent lengths of 256 tokens.

We compute cosine similarity using the all-MiniLM-L6-v211 1 https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model from the sentence-transformers library. This model generates 384-dimensional sentence embeddings for both the target and current responses. The cosine similarity is then computed between these embeddings, measuring semantic alignment at the sentence level rather than relying on surface-level token matching.

All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with 80GB memory.

For computing mean activations in different repatching strategies, we use the following datasets. For Harmful Patching, we use the first 100 adversarial instructions from AdvBench Zou et al. (2023). E.4 Training Convergence and Epoch Selection

Figure 6 analyzes the convergence behavior of GOSV optimization by tracking ASR as a function of training epochs across all four models. The curves demonstrate rapid ASR growth during the initial training phase, with most models achieving substantial performance gains within the first 300-500 epochs. Beyond this point, the improvement rate diminishes significantly, indicating that the optimization has effectively converged to identify the critical safety-related attention heads. Based on this convergence analysis, we select 500 epochs as the standard training configuration for GOSV in our experiments, which provides an optimal balance between attack effectiveness and computational efficiency.

To investigate the relationship between number of examples in Harmful Patching and attack effectiveness, we evaluate GOSV with varying numbers of training examples. Figure 7 presents the results on Llama-2-7B and Llama-3.1-8B.

Both models exhibit similar trends. ASR increases rapidly from 20 to 50 examples, then plateaus around 100 examples. This indicates that 100 training examples are sufficient for GOSV to identify safety vectors effectively, demonstrating the data efficiency of our approach.

Appendix F Scatter Plot Analysis of Safety Head Selection

Figure 8 visualizes the relationship between attention head selection probabilities under Harmful Patching (x-axis) and Zero Ablation (y-axis) across all four models. Each point represents an individual attention head (l,h)(l,h), positioned according to its optimized selection probability σ⁡(θ(l,h))\sigma(\theta^{(l,h)}) under both strategies. The scatter plots reveal a critical finding: the majority of points cluster along the axes rather than the diagonal, indicating that heads with high selection probability under one strategy typically have low selection probability under the other. This low correlation demonstrates that Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors exhibit minimal overlap, with most attention heads contributing primarily to one safety pathway rather than both. The consistent pattern across all four models confirms that this separation of safety mechanisms is a fundamental architectural property rather than a model-specific artifact.

Abstract
While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose G lobal O ptimization for S afety V ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

1 Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse domains. To mitigate the safety risks associated with such proficiency, prior work has aligned them with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Ouyang et al. (2022) and preference optimization like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Rafailov et al. (2023) . However, these safety guardrails are fragile, as models can still be compromised by various threats, including jailbreak attacks Zou et al. (2023) ; Liu et al. (2023) ; Zhu et al. (2024) ; Zhou et al. (2025) and model editing methods Arditi et al. (2024) . This vulnerability reveals our limited mechanistic understanding of the architectural components governing safety Zhao et al. (2024) ; Bereska and Gavves (2024) ; Lee et al. (2025) .
Revealing the internal safety mechanisms within black-box LLMs is commonly achieved through mechanistic interpretation methods. Some works map internal latent representations to interpretable concepts Zhou et al. (2024a) ; Pan et al. (2025b) ; Wollschläger et al. (2025) ; Zhao et al. (2025a) , enabling analysis of intermediate features and activation patterns related to safety behaviors. Recent studies use causal interventions to attribute safety-related behaviors to specific model components, such as safety layers Li et al. (2024) , safety neurons Chen et al. (2024) ; Zhao et al. (2025b) , or individual attention heads Zhou et al. (2024b) . However, these approaches typically rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. In reality, LLM components are highly interdependent—information flows dynamically across the network, and the function of one component fundamentally depends on others Elhage et al. (2022) ; Fakhar and Hilgetag (2022) ; Giallanza et al. (2024) . Consequently, local methods struggle to capture the emergent safety behaviors arising from such distributed interactions.
To uncover how components interact in maintaining safety, we propose G lobal O ptimization for S afety V ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety mechanisms through global optimization over all attention heads simultaneously. Inspired by Function Vectors Todd et al. (2023) , which posit that tasks are encoded as compact representations transportable by specific attention heads, we hypothesize that safety behaviors can be encoded as safety vectors across multiple heads. These safety vectors serve as implicit representations of safety mechanisms captured by sets of activations in the model. To comprehensively probe these safety mechanisms, we introduce two complementary activation repatching strategies that intervene from different perspectives. Harmful Patching injects mean activations computed from harmful content generation, capturing statistical signatures that trigger unsafe outputs. Zero Ablation suppresses information flow by zeroing head activations, eliminating safety-relevant signals.
Applying GOSV with these strategies, we obtain two sets of location-value pairs, which we term Malicious Injection Vectors (from Harmful Patching) and Safety Suppression Vectors (from Zero Ablation). Based on the identified safety vectors, we conduct systematic analyses to understand how attention heads influence model safety. These analyses reveal two critical findings. First, the two strategies identify spatially distinct sets of safety-critical heads with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain two separate functional pathways, both capable of independently compromising model safety. Second, complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total heads are repatched across all models, indicating that the identified safety vectors constitute roughly one-third of all attention heads and collectively govern model safety mechanisms. Case studies further validate this progressive safety breakdown by revealing the behavioral transitions from complete refusal to full compliance as the number of repatched heads approaches the 30% threshold.
Building on these insights, we develop an inference-time jailbreak method that replaces activations at identified safety-critical heads with corresponding repatching values. Critically, our attack requires no prompt engineering or query modification, operating purely through internal activation manipulation. Both strategies achieve complete safety breakdown, each independently compromising model safety. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks through inference-time interventions without parameter modifications, demonstrating that globally-attributed safety vectors enable more effective attacks.
Our work makes the following contributions:
•
We propose GOSV, a global optimization framework for identifying safety-critical attention heads. We discover two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors, providing empirical evidence of separate safety pathways in aligned LLMs.
•
We conduct systematic analyses to characterize how attention heads influence model safety, providing deeper understanding based on extensive experiments. Our findings advance the understanding of safety interpretability in LLMs.
•
We introduce an inference-time white-box jailbreak attack that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching, achieving superior attack performance across all models.

2 Related Work
2.1 Jailbreak Attacks in LLMs
Jailbreak attacks circumvent LLM safety alignment through diverse automated strategies. Early optimization approaches search for adversarial suffixes Zou et al. (2023) , later refined by dynamic objective alignment Zhu et al. (2024) and refusal suppression Zhou et al. (2025) . Semantic-focused methods employ genetic algorithms Liu et al. (2023) and iterative refinement Chao et al. (2025) ; Mehrotra et al. (2024) to generate human-readable prompts that bypass safety filters. Beyond single-turn prompts, attacks exploit complex contexts through nested simulations Li et al. (2023) , multi-turn escalation Russinovich et al. (2025) , or disguised intentions Zheng et al. (2025) . At the mechanistic level, recent work surgically disables safety constraints by orthogonalizing refusal directions Arditi et al. (2024) .
2.2 Safety Attribution in Attention Heads
Recent work identifies attention heads as critical architectural components governing LLM safety. Zhou et al. (2024b) introduced the Safety Head Importance Score, revealing that safety concentrates in sparse subsets of critical “safety heads.” Exploiting this sparsity, Hung et al. (2025) proposed Attention Tracker to detect prompt injection attacks by monitoring attention flow shifts. Li et al. (2025) introduced DeTAM for inference-time defense via targeted attention modification without retraining. Pan et al. (2025a) proposed AGD, adversarially refining attention weights through variable-sum games on jailbreak-sensitive heads to balance helpfulness and harmlessness. Banerjee et al. (2025) addressed multilingual safety alignment through language-specific head steering. However, these methods employ local, greedy attribution when identifying safety-critical heads, treating them as independent units and overlooking complex interdependencies. We address this via global optimization that simultaneously attributes safety across all attention heads.

We then describe two activation repatching strategies for interventions (§ 3.2 ), followed by the GOSV optimization algorithm that globally identifies safety vectors (§ 3.3 ). Finally, we introduce an inference-time jailbreak attack that exploits the identified safety vectors (§ 3.4 ).

4.1 Experiment Setting
Models.
We conduct experiments on four open-source LLMs with diverse architectures and alignment strategies: Llama-2-7b-chat Touvron et al. (2023) , Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Dubey et al. Datasets.
We employ two well-established benchmark datasets: AdvBench Zou et al. (2023) and StrongREJECT Souly et al. (2024) . To identify safety-critical heads, we use only 100 examples from AdvBench paired with corresponding harmful target responses. We then evaluate attack effectiveness on the complete AdvBench dataset (520 behaviors) and StrongREJECT dataset (313 malicious instructions) to assess generalization capability across diverse harmful scenarios.

4.3 The Optimal Intervention Range
To understand how safety mechanisms are distributed across attention heads, we systematically vary the number of repatched heads and measure ASR. We rank all attention heads by their optimized probability σ ⁡ ( θ ( l , h ) ) \sigma(\theta^{(l,h)}) in descending order and progressively apply repatching to the top- k k heads. As shown in Figure 4 , the ASR curves across four models exhibit three distinct phases:
Phase I: Critical Safety Heads Dominate.
The most striking observation is the rapid initial ASR growth with very few heads. For most models, ASR surges from near-zero to 50% or higher with only approximately 1% of total heads repatched. This steep initial slope demonstrates that a small subset of highly critical attention heads plays a disproportionate role in maintaining model safety. The effectiveness of GOSV’s global optimization is validated here, as it successfully identifies and ranks the most safety-critical heads at the top of the probability distribution. Notably, Qwen2.5 exhibits more gradual ASR growth, suggesting a more distributed safety architecture.
Phase II: Complete Safety Breakdown.
As we continue repatching heads in descending order of probability, ASR reaches its peak and plateaus at approximately 30% of total heads across all models and both strategies. This plateau represents the point where all safety-critical heads have been compromised, resulting in complete breakdown of safety mechanisms. The consistency of this 30% threshold across different model architectures and alignment strategies suggests a universal characteristic: safety in contemporary aligned LLMs is encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.
Phase III: Degraded Model Capabilities.
Beyond the optimal intervention point, some models exhibit slight ASR decline despite continued head repatching. This decline occurs not due to recovery of safety mechanisms, but because excessive intervention disrupts fundamental language generation capabilities. As shown in Figure 4 , perplexity measurements provide direct evidence. PPL remains stable during Phases I and II but rises sharply beyond the 30% threshold. When too many attention heads are repatched, outputs become incoherent and fail to meet the criteria for successful attacks even though safety barriers no longer function.
Case Study Analysis.
To understand the behavioral transitions underlying these quantitative patterns, we conduct a case study on Llama-3.1-8B with progressive head repatching using Zero Ablation. Table 1 presents output excerpts across different repatching intensities. With minimal intervention, the model provides complete refusals. As more heads are repatched, it displays conflicted behavior, maintaining refusal statements while progressively leaking harmful information. At approximately 30% repatched heads, the model transitions to full harmful compliance with detailed harmful instructions. Beyond this point, outputs become increasingly incoherent with repetitive tokens and random symbols. These behavioral transitions from complete refusal to full compliance validate the progressive safety breakdown characterized in our quantitative findings.
5 The Performance of Our Attack
Attack Effectiveness.
Table 2 compares the ASR of our attack and baseline methods across four LLMs on AdvBench and StrongREJECT benchmarks. For each model, we report the higher ASR achieved by either Harmful Patching or Zero Ablation strategy. Our attack achieves nearly the best performance across almost all model-dataset combinations, demonstrating its superior effectiveness. Specifically, our attack achieves near-perfect ASR on Mistral and Llama-3.1, substantially outperforming all baseline methods. On Llama-2-7B and Qwen2.5-7B, our attack also achieves competitive or superior performance compared to the strongest baselines. These results validate the efficacy of GOSV in discovering safety vectors and demonstrate our attack’s strong generalization capability across different model architectures and diverse harmful scenarios.
Validation with Alternative Activation Values.
To validate that our attack’s effectiveness stems from precisely targeting safety-critical mechanisms rather than arbitrary activation manipulation, we conduct a comprehensive study. Beyond our core strategies of Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation, we evaluate two alternative approaches: Benign Patching, using mean activations from benign instructions, and Random Patching, using randomly generated values. As shown in Figure 5 , only Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation achieve high ASR exceeding 90%. In contrast, Benign Patching and Random Patching show only marginal improvements over the vanilla model without intervention. These minimal gains stem from disrupting general model functionality rather than effectively compromising safety mechanisms. These results provide strong evidence that successful attacks require precisely targeting specific safety vectors.

We further compare our attack with a standard fine-tuning (FT) baseline that directly fine-tunes models using the same training data. As shown in Table 3 , while both methods achieve comparable performance on the training distribution (AdvBench), our attack demonstrates significantly superior generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios. These results highlight that by precisely targeting safety vectors through global optimization, our attack not only matches the effectiveness of parameter-modification approaches but also exhibits stronger generalization across diverse attack scenarios.
6 Conclusion
This work introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads. We discover two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways rather than a unified mechanism. Further analyses reveal that safety vectors are encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. Building on these insights, our inference-time attack achieves superior performance by repatching the identified safety vectors. Our findings challenge the monolithic view of safety alignment and reveal fundamental vulnerabilities in current approaches. This work advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and suggests that robust defenses must account for distributed, interdependent mechanisms across multiple pathways.
Limitations
While our work provides mechanistic insights into LLM safety through the GOSV framework, several limitations warrant discussion. First, we have not developed defense strategies to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities. Future work should focus on developing robust safeguards based on these insights. Second, our approach requires white-box access for activation patching, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios. Third, our evaluation focuses on a limited set of open-source models and English-language instructions. The generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors requires further investigation.
Ethical Considerations
Our research aims to advance the mechanistic understanding of safety mechanisms in LLMs. While the proposed attack demonstrates a method for bypassing safety guardrails, its primary purpose is to reveal the underlying vulnerabilities of current alignment techniques. We believe that identifying these distributed safety pathways is essential for developing more robust and resilient models. All experiments were conducted using publicly available benchmarks in controlled environments, and we adhere to the ethical guidelines for responsible AI research. We hope our findings encourage the development of more effective defense mechanisms to safeguard LLMs against adversarial exploitation.

Appendix C Details of Baselines
In this section, we summarize several representative jailbreak attack methods as baselines and, by comparing their core ideas, strengths, and limitations, provide a reference for the subsequent evaluation of our proposed method.
GCG. Zou et al. (2023) . GCG treats jailbreak as a discrete optimization problem over an adversarial suffix. It greedily updates one token per step to maximize the log-likelihood of a harmful target response, using token-level coordinate search rather than gradients.
AutoDAN Liu et al. (2023) . AutoDAN employs a hierarchical genetic algorithm to generate human-readable jailbreak prompts. Unlike token-level optimization, it operates at the semantic level through selection, crossover, and mutation of candidate prompts, achieving both effectiveness and interpretability.
AdvPrefix Zhu et al. (2024) . AdvPrefix identifies that traditional jailbreak objectives (forcing "Sure, here is…") are misspecified and overconstrained. It introduces a plug-and-play objective that dynamically selects model-dependent prefixes based on high prefilling attack success rates and low negative log-likelihood. This approach aligns the attack with the model’s natural generation probability, significantly smoothing the optimization landscape.
DSN Zhou et al. (2025) . DSN combines cosine decay scheduling with refusal suppression to achieve state-of-the-art attack success rates. It jointly optimizes two objectives: maximizing affirmative responses while minimizing refusal keywords, adaptively prioritizing initial tokens through cosine decay weighting to ensure both an affirmative start and sustained harmful generation throughout the response.
ORTHO Arditi et al. (2024) . ORTHO identifies "refusal directions" in the representation space and orthogonalizes activations with respect to these directions. It removes safety-relevant components through linear algebraic operations, enabling models to generate harmful content while maintaining coherence.

Appendix E Additional Experiment Details
E.1 Training Details
To obtain target harmful responses for GOSV optimization, we prompt unaligned base models with the corresponding harmful queries. These unaligned models naturally generate harmful content, providing reference outputs for our optimization process. During training, we ensure that the current generated responses and target responses maintain consistent lengths of 256 tokens.
We compute cosine similarity using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 1 1

https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model from the sentence-transformers library. This model generates 384-dimensional sentence embeddings for both the target and current responses. The cosine similarity is then computed between these embeddings, measuring semantic alignment at the sentence level rather than relying on surface-level token matching.
All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with 80GB memory.
E.2 Data for Computing Mean Activations
For computing mean activations in different repatching strategies, we use the following datasets. For Harmful Patching, we use the first 100 adversarial instructions from AdvBench Zou et al. (2023) . For Benign Patching (used in ablation studies), we use the first 100 benign instructions from Alpaca Taori et al. (2023) . For Random Patching, we generate random activation values sampled from a Gaussian distribution with the same mean and standard deviation as the harmful activations. E.4 Training Convergence and Epoch Selection
Figure 6 analyzes the convergence behavior of GOSV optimization by tracking ASR as a function of training epochs across all four models. The curves demonstrate rapid ASR growth during the initial training phase, with most models achieving substantial performance gains within the first 300-500 epochs. Beyond this point, the improvement rate diminishes significantly, indicating that the optimization has effectively converged to identify the critical safety-related attention heads. Based on this convergence analysis, we select 500 epochs as the standard training configuration for GOSV in our experiments, which provides an optimal balance between attack effectiveness and computational efficiency.
E.5 Impact of Number of Examples in Harmful Patching
To investigate the relationship between number of examples in Harmful Patching and attack effectiveness, we evaluate GOSV with varying numbers of training examples. Figure 7 presents the results on Llama-2-7B and Llama-3.1-8B.
Both models exhibit similar trends. ASR increases rapidly from 20 to 50 examples, then plateaus around 100 examples. This indicates that 100 training examples are sufficient for GOSV to identify safety vectors effectively, demonstrating the data efficiency of our approach.

Appendix F Scatter Plot Analysis of Safety Head Selection
Figure 8 visualizes the relationship between attention head selection probabilities under Harmful Patching (x-axis) and Zero Ablation (y-axis) across all four models. Each point represents an individual attention head ( l , h ) (l,h) , positioned according to its optimized selection probability σ ⁡ ( θ ( l , h ) ) \sigma(\theta^{(l,h)}) under both strategies. The scatter plots reveal a critical finding: the majority of points cluster along the axes rather than the diagonal, indicating that heads with high selection probability under one strategy typically have low selection probability under the other. This low correlation demonstrates that Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors exhibit minimal overlap, with most attention heads contributing primarily to one safety pathway rather than both. The consistent pattern across all four models confirms that this separation of safety mechanisms is a fundamental architectural property rather than a model-specific artifact.
